title: How should armies fight? - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: A review of Jack Watling's 'The Arms of the Future', arguing that improving sensor reach, weapon range and munition precision have made massed concentration and surprise impossible, leaving armies to dig in, retreat to cities, or fight the sensors directly. The Ukraine war has evolved as Watling predicted, with defenders underground or in cities and attackers suffering heavy losses unless they first blind enemy sensors.

themes.theme: Sensors, range and precision end massed maneuver

insights.claim: Jack Watling's 'The Arms of the Future' (2023) argues that three improving forces define modern war: the reach of sensors, the range of weapons, and the precision of munitions, which together have made previous ways of fighting impossible.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Defense spending should tilt toward sensors, long-range fires and precision munitions rather than legacy massed-armor platforms.
insights.quote: three forces define war today: the reach of sensors, the range of weapons, and the precision of munitions
insights.locator: Jack Watling may have written another

insights.claim: Heavy artillery accuracy has improved dramatically: eighty years ago it missed by an average of fifty meters at sixteen kilometers, while in tests today it misses by an average of two meters at seventy kilometers.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Precision-guided artillery and munitions makers benefit as accuracy at range becomes decisive.
insights.quote: heavy artillery firing at seventy kilometers misses by an average of just two meters

insights.claim: Rocket artillery and kamikaze drones regularly hit targets at roughly twice the range of today's heavy artillery (around 140 km versus 70 km).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Supports sustained demand for rocket artillery and loitering munitions.
insights.quote: Other weapons like rocket artillery and kamikaze drones regularly hit targets at twice that range

insights.claim: Cheap, diverse sensors now find targets: consumer-drone cameras, commercial satellites, ground surveillance radars, soldier-carried acoustic sensors that can identify a tank from ten kilometers, and laser or electronic-emission detection of heartbeats and phone calls.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Commercial satellite imagery, drone and signals-intelligence suppliers sit at the center of the new battlefield.
insights.quote: an acoustic sensor carried by a single soldier can identify a tank from ten kilometers away

insights.claim: Because a radar operator can spot vehicles assembling from fifty kilometers away and artillery can strike minutes later, the generals' traditional combination of surprise and concentration has become impossible, a problem that applies to Western militaries too.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Western force structures built around armored concentration may be obsolete, implying large doctrinal and procurement shifts.
insights.quote: both are impossible if a radar operator can spot vehicles assembling from fifty kilometers away

insights.claim: In Ukraine, grouping vehicles within a few tens of kilometers of the front often gets them destroyed, and this 'gray zone' keeps expanding into what used to be the rear as sensors and munitions improve.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A widening kill zone raises demand for dispersion, deep strike and counter-sensor capabilities.
insights.quote: As sensors and munitions improve, this ‘gray zone’ keeps growing, reaching far into what used to be the rear.

themes.theme: Three options: dig in, go urban, or blind the enemy

insights.claim: Armies' first option against pervasive sensing is to disperse and harden by digging in, which works well for defense but makes any attack piecemeal and bloody.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Defense-dominant battlefields favor attritional, long wars and fortification spending.
insights.quote: This is a great tactic when defending, but ensures that any attack they mount will be piecemeal and bloody.

insights.claim: The second option is retreating into cities, which act like a warren of shelters preserving mobility, but an army that ignores the countryside risks being surrounded and still cannot attack.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Urban warfare capabilities and specialized assault units gain importance.
insights.quote: To the modern soldier, the urban environment is like a warren of tunnels

insights.claim: Watling's preferred option is to restore movement and surprise by fighting the sensors: small, highly mobile groups that destroy enemy sensors and deploy their own, backed by heavy artillery further back and specialized assault units for cities and strongpoints, aiming only for brief windows to seize single objectives rather than long Guderian-style offensives.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Counter-ISR, electronic warfare and anti-drone systems become the enabler of any offensive and a key procurement priority.
insights.quote: create a brief window in which troops can assemble and take a single objective without being spotted and destroyed
insights.locator: Their third option, and Watling’s preference

insights.claim: The Ukraine war has evolved as Watling predicted: most Ukrainian soldiers live underground for months, hundreds of meters from the nearest friendly unit, avoid movement, and prefer to hold towns and cities such as Pokrovsk and Kostyantynivka.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Expect continued slow, attritional front lines rather than rapid breakthroughs, relevant to ceasefire and reconstruction timelines.
insights.quote: Most Ukrainian soldiers live underground, sometimes for months at a time

insights.claim: A Ukrainian battalion commander told Watling he needs buildings to fight from rather than reinforcements, illustrating urban terrain as the decisive defensive asset.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Urban terrain matters more than manpower in defense, shaping where fronts stall.
insights.quote: ‘I don’t need reinforcements, I need buildings to fight from.’
insights.locator: The Arms of the Future came

insights.claim: Attacking Russian forces, unable to dig in, shelter in cities, concentrate or achieve surprise, are suffering astonishing losses.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Attrition rates bear on Russia's sustainability of the war and its defense-industrial demand.
insights.locator: The Arms of the Future came

insights.claim: Some Ukrainian units, such as the Third Assault Brigade, succeed by first targeting enemy sensors before grouping and rushing forward, but this only works while they can keep blinding the enemy, and continued sensor and munition improvement may close even this option.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Counter-sensor capabilities are a moving target; offense-defense balance could tilt further toward defense, implying static wars.
insights.quote: they will succeed only as long as they manage to keep blinding the enemy
